title: Sedgwick County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sedgwick County wells have a 100 ft median depth. Compare local yields, water levels and modeled finished-well costs of $9,500-$17,500.
h1: Sedgwick County wells: what to expect before you buy
intro_html:
A shallow well and a deep drilling bill are both possible in Sedgwick County. The recorded median depth is 100 ft, but the middle half runs from 57-320 ft. That spread matters more to a land buyer than the county average would.

Colorado DWR records include 2,264 permitted wells countywide, with 1,311 recorded as constructed. Use those records to start your research around Julesburg, Ovid or Sedgwick, then narrow the comparison to nearby wells with similar uses and aquifer information. A permit record alone does not establish that a working well exists today.

sections.heading: A 100 ft median hides a wide Sedgwick County depth range
sections.html:
Of the 1,492 wells reporting depth, the median is 100 ft and the middle half spans 57-320 ft. For a drilling bid, that means the median is a starting allowance, not a reliable target for every parcel. The 90th-percentile depth is 380 ft.

Local ground includes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name the Ogallala for 338 wells and Alluvial for 31; another 1,788 fall in the unnamed / fractured-bedrock category. That broad record label does not establish fractured rock beneath your lot. Ask the driller to compare nearby completion logs, water-bearing intervals and casing requirements before setting a depth allowance.

sections.heading: Strong reported yields, but not a household-well promise
sections.html:
The 302 wells with pump-yield records have a median of 50.0 gpm, with a middle half of 15.0-900.0 gpm. Those figures cover different well uses: irrigation accounts for 34% of county permit records, domestic/household 29% and stock 27%. Do not treat the county yield median as a prediction for a new home well.

No reported yields fall below 1 gpm, while 2% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. That is encouraging within the reporting sample, but it does not rule out poor production or dry holes. For a purchase, request a current pumping and recovery test. Also verify permitted uses; a productive well does not automatically authorize lawn watering, livestock or irrigation.

sections.heading: Water stands at 40 ft in the median record—not everywhere
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to resting water, not the total drilled depth. Only 112 county wells report it. Their median is 40 ft below ground, and the middle half runs from 18-216 ft. That range matters when evaluating pump placement and lift, although pumping conditions require their own measurements.

Decade medians are 218 ft in the 1970s, 39 ft in the 2010s and 52 ft in the 2020s. The latest median is deeper than the preceding one, but this is not a same-well monitoring series. Different locations, aquifers and reporting samples prevent a defensible countywide claim that the water table is steadily dropping. Look for repeat measurements near the property.

sections.heading: Sedgwick County permit history and recorded drillers
sections.html:
The permit history extends from 142 issuances in the 1950s to a newest permit year of 2025. The 2000s account for 299 permits, followed by 205 in the 2010s and 97 in the 2020s. The latest decade is incomplete, so its smaller count is not a fair measure of a long-term slowdown.

The most active drillers in the records are Jim Feighny & Sons with 184, Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc with 177, and Haggard Drilling Inc. with 158. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. When requesting bids, ask about experience in your part of the county and the aquifer expected beneath the lot.

sections.heading: Budget beyond the drilled hole near Julesburg, Ovid or Sedgwick
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for drilling in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 100 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,500-$5,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $9,500-$17,500.

That finished-well range is a planning figure tied to the median depth, not a parcel quote. The 57-320 ft middle-half depth range leaves substantial room for a different drilling bill. Have bidders spell out casing, grout, development, testing and what happens if drilling must continue deeper. Check trench routes, electrical service and rig access before comparing prices; a hole-only quote and a working-water-system quote are not equivalent.

sections.heading: Check water quality and well condition before closing
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental inventory lists 5 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site. Those map entries do not establish contamination in a particular well, but they justify checking site details and choosing testing appropriate to the property. The inventory lists no historic mine features; that does not establish safe drinking water.

Have a qualified laboratory test the well water, including bacteria and nitrate, and discuss PFAS testing based on nearby site information. Inspect the wellhead, casing condition and drainage, and review septic placement. Strong county yield figures cannot substitute for an individual production test, and permit records cannot establish a parcel's dry-hole risk.

sections.heading: Make the lot work before committing to the well
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel and its DWR permit status, then review neighboring wells around Julesburg, Ovid or Sedgwick. Phillips County is nearby, but crossing a county line is less important than matching local geology, aquifer and intended use. Ask for completion logs rather than relying only on map symbols.

For an existing home, match the permit to the physical well and confirm that its authorized uses fit your plans. For vacant land, confirm permit eligibility with DWR before assuming a household-use well is available; augmentation requirements may affect proposed uses. Lay out the house, septic system, driveway, well and utility routes together. Keep drilling access and future pump-service access open in the site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sedgwick County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 100 ft, and the middle half of wells runs from 57-320 ft. Those figures come from 1,492 depth records countywide. Local aquifer conditions matter more than the median for an individual lot, so compare nearby completion logs before using a depth allowance in a drilling budget.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sedgwick County?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 100 ft median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $3,500-$5,500 and a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical at about $9,500-$17,500. Deeper drilling and site-specific installation requirements can change the bid. Ask for an itemized scope rather than a hole-only price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Sedgwick County?
faq.a: Among 302 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 50.0 gpm and the middle half is 15.0-900.0 gpm. The county records include irrigation and stock wells as well as household wells, so those yields are not a household-well guarantee. Get a current pumping and recovery test, and check that the permit authorizes your intended uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sedgwick County?
faq.a: County permit statistics cannot establish drinking-water safety. The nearby environmental inventory includes 5 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund/cleanup site within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not prove a well is affected. Test the property's water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby site information, wellhead condition and septic placement.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Sedgwick County?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a steady countywide decline. Median static water depths are 218 ft for the 1970s, 39 ft for the 2010s and 52 ft for the 2020s. These are measurements from potentially different wells and aquifers, not repeated readings from a fixed monitoring network. Seek local repeat measurements before drawing conclusions.
